modes.blurb: The whole final paper, in order: pairing polygons, true/false, grape ↔ country, designation ↔ country.
modes.why: Same order and weight as the final: Part 1 (5 pts) completes food-and-wine polygons, Part 2 (10 pts) is ten true/false items on the sessions after the midterm, Parts 3 and 4 (5 pts each) are one five-pair match each. Each run prefers what you have not mastered yet.

modes.title: Final exam part 1: Wine & food pairing

parts.title: Final exam part 1: Wine & food pairing

modes.blurb: A dish or a wine on the AIS pairing chart: complete the other polygon, or read the result.
modes.why: Freshly generated every time. Each wine axis faces the food it balances: acidity ↔ sweet tendency and fattiness, alcohol/tannin ↔ juiciness and oiliness, softness ↔ salt, bitter and sour, intensity ↔ persistence and spice.

modes.title: Final exam part 2: True or false

parts.title: Final exam part 2: True or false

modes.blurb: Wine Servicing, Beers & Distillates and Delicatessen as true/false.
modes.why: A false statement is a true one with one fact swapped for its neighbour: left for right, aerobic for anaerobic, Normandy for Gascogne. Learn the pairs, not the gist.

modes.title: Final exam part 3: Grape ↔ country
modes.blurb: Five grapes, a pool of countries with spares.
modes.why: Every pool has spare countries, so the last pair never falls out by elimination. Only grapes tied to one country on the slides are used.

modes.title: Final exam part 4: Designation ↔ country or grape

parts.title: Final exam part 4: Designation ↔ country or grape

modes.blurb: Designations from Europe and the New World, matched to country or grape.
modes.why: Rioja, Tokaji and Marlborough sit beside Barolo and Chablis: the paper can draw on any producer deck.
